description_full: Cirrus Logic, Inc., a fabless semiconductor company, develops mixed-signal processing solutions and audio products in China, the United States, and internationally. The company offers audio products, including amplifiers; codecs components that integrate analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) and digital-to-analog converters (DACs) into a single integrated circuit (IC); smart codecs, a codec with integrated digital signal processing; standalone digital signal processors; and SoundClear technology for use in smartphones, PCs, tablets, AR/VR headsets, wearables, home theatre systems, automotive entertainment systems, and professional audio systems. It also provides camera controllers, haptic and sensing solutions, and battery and power ICs for smartphones, as well as products for automotive, industrial, and imaging applications. The company markets and sells its products through direct sales force, external sales representatives, and distributors. Cirrus Logic, Inc. was incorporated in 1984 and is headquartered in Austin, Texas.

financial_summary: Cirrus Logic, Inc. is a mid-cap technology business with a $5.7B market cap on $2.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 22% against a 10% cost of capital — a 12-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 50% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $637M in free cash flow — roughly 32 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.57× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -9.5% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
